title: Fritsch, Hitzig, Penfield and brain maps (Bridge to AI: modularity versus distributed representations)
text:
CHAPTER 3. LOCALIZING FUNCTION
SECTION 3.3. FRITSCH, HITZIG, PENFIELD, AND BRAIN MAPS

From lesions to stimulation

Broca and Wernicke showed what happens when parts of the cortex are destroyed. The next step was to ask what happens when parts of the cortex are activated. If you could stimulate a small spot of cortex and see a specific response, you would have direct evidence that the spot is involved in that function. This is the logic of the stimulation method, which complements the lesion method. In engineering terms, lesions are like removing a component, and stimulation is like injecting a test signal.

Before 1870, many physiologists believed that the cerebral cortex was electrically inexcitable. Earlier attempts to stimulate the cortex had generally failed to produce clear movements, perhaps because of inadequate stimulation methods or anesthesia. The prevailing view, influenced by Flourens, was that the cortex was the seat of the will and of perception, but that it did not directly control specific muscles.

Fritsch and Hitzig, 1870

In 1870, two German physicians in Berlin, Gustav Fritsch (1838 to 1927) and Eduard Hitzig (1838 to 1907), published a paper that overturned this view. Both had prior interest in the topic. Hitzig had noticed, while applying electric currents to the heads of patients for therapeutic purposes, that stimulating the back of the head could cause eye movements. Fritsch, according to an often repeated story, had observed muscle twitches when he touched the exposed brain of a soldier with a head wound while dressing it during the Prussian-Danish war. (Such stories are hard to verify, but they appear in many histories.)

Their experiments were carried out on dogs, reportedly at first in Hitzig's home because suitable laboratory space was not available. They exposed the cortex and applied weak direct currents from a battery through fine electrodes. They found that stimulating specific small areas in the front part of the cortex caused movements of specific body parts on the opposite side of the body: the foreleg, the hindleg, the face, the neck. Stimulating other areas of cortex caused no movements. Moreover, when they removed the area from which forelimb movements could be evoked, the dog's use of that forelimb was impaired, though not abolished.

This was the first strong experimental evidence for a motor cortex, and for localization of function in the cortex based on direct manipulation rather than clinical correlation. It also showed that the cortex is electrically excitable. Their paper, often referred to by its German title, Uber die elektrische Erregbarkeit des Grosshirns ("On the electrical excitability of the cerebrum"), is a landmark in neuroscience.

Hughlings Jackson and the march of seizures

Around the same time, the English neurologist John Hughlings Jackson (1835 to 1911) was reaching a similar conclusion from clinical observation. He studied patients with a type of epilepsy in which a seizure begins with twitching in one part of the body, for example the fingers of one hand, and then spreads in a regular order: from the fingers to the wrist, the arm, the shoulder, and sometimes the face and leg. This spreading pattern is now called the "Jacksonian march."

Jackson reasoned that the seizure was an abnormal electrical discharge starting at one point in the cortex and spreading to adjacent areas. If the spread of the seizure across the body follows a consistent order, then adjacent body parts must be represented in adjacent areas of cortex. In other words, the motor cortex must contain an orderly map of the body. This was an inference made before the experimental proof, and Fritsch and Hitzig's results, along with Ferrier's, supported it.

Jackson also proposed influential ideas about the hierarchical organization of the nervous system, in which higher levels control and inhibit lower levels. When higher levels are damaged, he argued, lower-level, more automatic behaviors may be "released." This hierarchical view anticipates ideas in modern motor control and in robotics, where high-level planners send commands to lower-level controllers that handle details.

David Ferrier and monkeys

David Ferrier (1843 to 1928), a Scottish neurologist working in London, extended the stimulation experiments in the 1870s, using a variety of animals, including monkeys. He used alternating current from an induction coil (faradic stimulation), which was more effective at evoking sustained movements than the brief direct current pulses of Fritsch and Hitzig. Ferrier mapped motor areas in detail and also tried to locate sensory areas, such as those for vision and hearing, using both stimulation and lesions. His book The Functions of the Brain (1876) was very influential. Some of his sensory localizations were wrong (for example, his early placement of the visual area), but his motor maps were broadly correct.

Ferrier's work also became the center of a public controversy. At the International Medical Congress in London in 1881, he presented a monkey with a motor cortex lesion that showed paralysis consistent with his maps, in a debate with the German physiologist Friedrich Goltz, who argued against strict localization with dogs that had large cortical lesions but retained many functions. Ferrier was then prosecuted under the new Cruelty to Animals Act of 1876 for performing experiments without a license; the case was dismissed when it was shown that the experiments had been done by a licensed colleague, Gerald Yeo. This episode is a reminder that the ethics of animal research have been debated for as long as experimental neuroscience has existed.

Cytoarchitecture: Brodmann's map

While physiologists mapped function, anatomists mapped structure. Under the microscope, the cerebral cortex is made of layers of cells, conventionally six layers in most of the neocortex. The thickness of each layer, the density and size of neurons, and the types of cells vary from one region to another. Anatomists realized that these differences could be used to divide the cortex into distinct areas.

The most famous such map was published by the German neuroanatomist Korbinian Brodmann (1868 to 1918) in 1909. Based on the arrangement of cells (cytoarchitecture), Brodmann divided the human cortex into numbered areas. His numbering, which runs from 1 to 52 but omits some numbers in humans, is still used today. For example:

- Area 4 is the primary motor cortex, in the precentral gyrus, identified by very large pyramidal neurons (Betz cells) in layer 5.
- Areas 3, 1, and 2 make up the primary somatosensory cortex, in the postcentral gyrus.
- Area 17 is the primary visual cortex, in the occipital lobe, which has a prominent stripe of fibers in layer 4 (the stria of Gennari) that can be seen with the naked eye in sections.
- Areas 41 and 42 are in the auditory cortex.
- Areas 44 and 45 roughly correspond to Broca's area.

Brodmann believed that areas with different structure would have different functions, and in many cases this has turned out to be true. His map was a hypothesis about functional organization derived from anatomy. Modern parcellations combine cytoarchitecture, connectivity, functional imaging, and other data. A notable example is the multimodal parcellation of the human cortex published by Matthew Glasser and colleagues in 2016, using data from the Human Connectome Project, which identified 180 areas per hemisphere.

Wilder Penfield and the human cortex

The most famous maps of the human cortex came from neurosurgery. Wilder Penfield (1891 to 1976), an American-born neurosurgeon who worked in Montreal, founded the Montreal Neurological Institute in 1934. He developed a surgical treatment for epilepsy that involved removing the small area of cortex where seizures began. To avoid damaging critical functions, he needed to know what each area of exposed cortex did in that individual patient.

Penfield's "Montreal procedure" used local anesthesia so that the patient could remain awake during surgery. The brain itself has no pain receptors, so once the scalp, skull, and membranes are anesthetized and opened, the cortex can be touched without pain. Penfield then stimulated points on the cortex with a weak electrical current and asked the patient to report what they felt, or watched what moved. He placed small numbered tickets on the cortex to mark the points and photographed them, creating a precise record. This technique, in modern form, is still used in neurosurgery today and is called intraoperative electrical stimulation mapping or cortical stimulation mapping.

From many patients, Penfield and his colleagues built maps of the motor and somatosensory cortex. They summarized these maps in drawings of a distorted human figure laid along the cortex: the "homunculus" (little man). The first version appeared in a 1937 paper by Penfield and Edwin Boldrey, and a better known version appeared in the 1950 book The Cerebral Cortex of Man by Penfield and Theodore Rasmussen. The homunculus has very large hands, lips, and tongue, and a small trunk and legs. This reflects the fact that the amount of cortex devoted to a body part is proportional not to its size but to the precision of control or sensitivity it requires. The hands and the mouth, used for fine manipulation and speech, get a large share.

Key properties of these maps:

- Somatotopy: the body is mapped in an orderly way, with adjacent body parts mostly represented in adjacent cortex, as Jackson predicted. The sequence along the central sulcus, roughly from the top of the brain down the side, goes from toes and leg, through trunk, arm and hand, to face, lips, tongue, and throat.
- Contralateral control: each hemisphere controls and senses mainly the opposite side of the body.
- Magnification: important body parts have disproportionately large representations.
- Discontinuities: the map is not perfectly continuous; for example, the hand area lies next to the face area.

The details of the homunculus have been criticized and refined. Later work has shown that the motor cortex map is more overlapping and less sharply segregated than the classic drawing suggests, and that stimulating with longer trains of pulses can evoke complex coordinated movements rather than simple twitches. Michael Graziano and colleagues reported in the early 2000s that long stimulation trains in monkey motor cortex can evoke complex, goal-like movements, such as bringing the hand to the mouth, organized into a map of behavioral repertoire. In 2023, a study by Evan Gordon, Nico Dosenbach, and colleagues using precision fMRI reported that the classic motor strip contains, interleaved between effector regions for foot, hand, and mouth, regions they named the "somato-cognitive action network," linked to whole-body action planning and to brain networks for arousal and goals. Such findings refine rather than discard Penfield's basic picture.

Experiential responses

Penfield also reported that stimulation of the temporal lobes in some epilepsy patients produced vivid "experiential responses": patients reported hearing music, seeing familiar scenes, or having a feeling of reliving a past event. Penfield interpreted some of these as the reactivation of stored memories. This interpretation has been questioned. Such responses were rare, occurred mainly in patients with temporal lobe epilepsy, and could be reconstructions or dreamlike experiences rather than faithful replays. But the observations were important evidence that the temporal lobe is involved in memory and experience, and they influenced later research on memory, including the study of the patient H.M., whom we meet in chapter 9.

Maps everywhere

After the motor and somatosensory maps, neuroscientists found that maps are a general feature of the brain:

- Retinotopic maps in visual cortex, where neighboring points in the visual field are represented by neighboring points in cortex. There are many such maps in the visual cortex, one in each visual area.
- Tonotopic maps in auditory cortex, where sound frequency is mapped in order across the cortex, reflecting the frequency map along the cochlea.
- Maps of space in the superior colliculus, which help direct eye movements.

These topographic maps are thought to make computation efficient. If neurons that represent nearby points need to interact, placing them close together keeps the wiring short. This "wiring minimization" principle has been proposed as one explanation for cortical organization.

Bridge to AI: maps, stimulation, and self-organization

Several ideas in this section have strong parallels in AI and machine learning.

Self-organizing maps. In the 1980s, the Finnish engineer Teuvo Kohonen developed the self-organizing map (SOM), a neural network algorithm that learns to arrange units on a two-dimensional sheet so that nearby units respond to similar inputs. A SOM trained on inputs from different body parts would develop a somatotopic map; trained on sounds of different frequencies, it would develop a tonotopic map. Kohonen's work was explicitly inspired by cortical maps and by earlier theoretical work on how such maps might develop, including models by Christoph von der Malsburg in the 1970s. More recent work has shown that adding a spatial "wiring cost" or topographic constraint to deep networks can produce maps resembling those in visual cortex, including clustered category-selective regions such as face-preferring patches.

Magnification and resource allocation. The homunculus devotes more cortex to the hands and lips because those regions need higher resolution. In machine learning and signal processing, adaptive resolution is common: attention mechanisms allocate more computation to more important parts of an input; foveated rendering in VR allocates more pixels where the eye is looking; and in robotics, tactile sensor arrays in robot hands are often denser at the fingertips, just like human skin.

Stimulation as causal testing. Penfield's stimulation is a causal intervention: activate a component and see what happens. In AI interpretability, researchers use analogous "activation steering" or "activation patching" methods: they add a vector to a network's internal activations, or copy activations from one input to another, and observe how the output changes. If adding a particular direction makes a language model talk more about a certain topic, that is evidence that the direction represents that topic. This is the Penfield method applied to a neural network.

Hierarchical control. Jackson's idea that higher levels control and inhibit lower levels is the basis of hierarchical control in robotics: a high-level planner chooses goals, a mid-level controller generates trajectories, and low-level controllers drive motors. In hierarchical reinforcement learning, an agent learns policies at multiple time scales, with high-level policies choosing subgoals for low-level policies. A robot arm whose high-level controller fails may still exhibit stable low-level reflexes, like a patient whose higher centers are damaged.

Summary

- In 1870, Fritsch and Hitzig showed that electrical stimulation of specific areas of dog cortex produces movements on the opposite side of the body, establishing the motor cortex.
- Hughlings Jackson inferred from the march of focal seizures that the motor cortex contains an orderly map of the body, and he proposed a hierarchical organization of the nervous system.
- Ferrier extended stimulation mapping to monkeys; Brodmann divided the cortex into numbered areas based on cell structure (1909).
- Penfield used electrical stimulation in awake patients during epilepsy surgery to map human motor and sensory cortex, producing the homunculus.
- Topographic maps are found throughout the brain; modern work refines rather than rejects them.
- Self-organizing maps, attention, activation steering, and hierarchical control are AI parallels of these discoveries.
